title: Zhu Rongji’s “Big Move” - The Wire China
gist: An excerpt from Adam Y. Liu's 'Authoritarian Markets' argues that Zhu Rongji bought local-government consent for the 1994 fiscal recentralization — which lifted the center's revenue share from 22 percent to over 56 percent in one year — by secretly granting provinces and cities the right to found their own banks, an under-recognized grand bargain that created China's diversified local-bank sector and its later local-debt problem.

insights.claim: China's central government share of total government revenue jumped from just 22 percent in 1993 to well over 56 percent in 1994 as a result of the fiscal recentralization Zhu Rongji drove through.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: One of the sharpest single-year shifts in fiscal power in modern economic history — the benchmark for what Beijing can achieve when it decides to reallocate resources.
insights.quote: The center’s share of government revenue increased from just 22 percent in 1993 to well over 56 percent in 1994.
insights.locator: We know that, in the end, Beijing did get by

insights.claim: Fiscal recentralization halted a seventeen-year decline in China's revenue-to-GDP ratio that had been caused largely by localities maximizing their own fiscal surpluses.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Shows the state's extractive capacity is a policy choice, not a structural ceiling — relevant to any thesis that Beijing is fiscally constrained today.
insights.locator: Fiscal recentralization also halted a seventeen-year decline

insights.claim: Fiscal recentralization was the most critical of Zhu's reforms because without it Beijing could not have undertaken SOE reform or withstood the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Sequencing insight: fiscal capacity is the precondition for absorbing reform pain and external shocks — a template for assessing which reforms China can attempt now.
insights.locator: Of all the reforms Zhu oversaw, the most critical was fiscal recentralization

insights.claim: Zhu warned in 1993 that the central government's finances were unsustainable and that without suitably centralizing revenues Beijing would not be able to get by.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Documents that the reform was driven by near-crisis fiscal distress, not grand design — crises, not plans, unlock Chinese structural reform.
insights.quote: The central government’s finances are in very poor shape, to the point of being unsustainable… If we don’t suitably centralize revenues… we won’t be able to get by.
insights.locator: As vice premier in the early 1990s

insights.claim: From January to September 1993 local government revenues grew 18 percent while central revenues grew only 0.9 percent, the divergence Zhu used to justify reclaiming fiscal powers he said localities had chipped away.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A 20x growth gap between local and central revenue is the quantitative trigger to watch for when forecasting future recentralization pushes.
insights.quote: local revenues grew by 18 percent, in sharp contrast to only 0.9 percent growth in central revenues
insights.locator: Zhu’s concern was well founded

insights.claim: Recentralization made localities unambiguously worse off: their revenue share fell while their share of total expenditures kept growing, and the center continued issuing unfunded mandates such as construction blueprints localities had to fund themselves.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The structural revenue-expenditure mismatch dated to 1994 is the root cause of China's later land-finance and LGFV debt build-up.
insights.locator: When we consider just the budgetary revenue and expenditure part

themes.theme: Bargaining, not fiat: how the reform passed

insights.claim: Before triggering recentralization Zhu led a team of seventy central bureaucrats to seventeen provinces in ten weeks, arguing the case province by province rather than imposing the reform administratively.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Contradicts the model of Chinese policy as top-down decree; major reforms require negotiated buy-in, which is why they are slow and why announced targets often slip.
insights.locator: Leading a team of seventy central bureaucrats

insights.claim: The fiercest resistance to recentralization came from the rich provinces that had benefited most from the old fiscal arrangement, with Guangdong 'crossing swords' with Zhu across three meetings and initially refusing to give an inch.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Wealthy-coastal-province resistance is the recurring veto point in Chinese redistribution — the same dynamic constrains today's common-prosperity and transfer-payment agendas.
insights.locator: Localities initially still resisted fiercely

insights.claim: Zhu declined to fire resistant local officials, treating that as a clumsy exercise of authoritarian power, and instead cajoled and appeased them.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reusable model: authoritarian systems that rely on purges for compliance destroy the local incentives they need for growth — a lens for reading Xi-era enforcement costs.
insights.quote: Did Zhu fire the local officials? No, he did not. That would have been a clumsy exercise of authoritarian power.
insights.locator: Did Zhu fire the local officials?

insights.claim: Zhu promised localities that Beijing would not inquire into their overall revenues and expenditures — calling these their 'private secrets' — and that they could spend their money however they saw fit, which is why the center did not begin auditing localities until 2013.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A nineteen-year audit blind spot from 1994 to 2013 explains why the true scale of local government debt was unknown for so long and why data on it remains unreliable.
insights.locator: In addition to promising using fiscal transfers

themes.theme: Bank licenses as the hidden currency

insights.claim: The core of the new central-local pact was Zhu giving local governments the green light to set up their own banks, a concession first floated at the 1993 national conference on economic work after his seventy-day national tour.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reframes China's local banking sector as a political side-payment rather than a financial-development policy — which is why its credit quality tracks local fiscal stress.
insights.quote: Most importantly, Zhu gave local governments the green light to set up their own banks.
insights.locator: Most importantly, Zhu gave local governments the green light

insights.claim: Zhu explicitly told central bankers on August 15, 1994 that he had been hinting at a 'big move' in banking reform, namely setting up local banks, and that they need not fear local governments running them because the new banks would still operate under central bank regulations.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Documentary proof the local-bank explosion was deliberate central policy, not local improvisation — it implies Beijing owns the resulting balance-sheet problem.
insights.quote: I’ve been hinting at a ‘big move’ in our banking reform — that is, setting up local banks.
insights.locator: Zhu concluded by saying

insights.claim: Zhu used the same bank-license bargaining chip again ahead of the 1998 Big 4 reform, telling officials in 1997 that while the center deepened reform of Big 4 bank management it must simultaneously speed up establishing local banks whose Party organizations would all be local.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Confirms a repeatable pattern: every centralizing financial reform in China is paid for with a decentralizing licensing concession — watch for the concession whenever Beijing centralizes.
insights.quote: at the same time that we deepen reforms of the bank management system [of the Big 4], we must speed up the establishment of local banks
insights.locator: Zhu’s subsequent remarks are yet another smoking gun

insights.claim: Banks proliferated in China immediately after 1994 and the new locally led banks became ferocious competitors to the Big 4, permanently reshaping the industry into a more diversified and competitive market inside party-state bounds.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The competitive fragmentation of Chinese banking was an accident of political appeasement — explains persistent thin margins and weak underwriting discipline at the local-bank tier.
insights.locator: Zhu kept his word. Banks proliferated in China right after 1994

insights.claim: Letting local governments into banking was understood at the time to invite abuse by local officials, but Zhu accepted that trade-off because nothing was more urgent than fixing the fiscal system.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A known, deliberately accepted moral hazard — investors should treat China's local-bank credit risk as a legacy political cost rather than a supervisory failure.
insights.quote: Any pact is a trade-off, be it fiscal or not, and nothing was more urgent back then for Beijing than getting the fiscal system fixed.
insights.locator: Those who study banking and Socialist economies

insights.claim: Zhu's use of bank licenses for appeasement remains largely unknown because the internal discussions only became public with his 2013 memoir, and even bankers with decades of experience believed local state banks were purely local initiatives.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A widely held factual error among practitioners means consensus models of Chinese bank formation are wrong at the root — an information edge for anyone analyzing the sector's origins.
insights.quote: it simply cannot be possible that Zhu Rongji allowed these banks to exist in the first place
insights.locator: Few know that Zhu used bank licenses for appeasement

insights.claim: In 1996 Beijing asserted unprecedented control over local extrabudgetary revenue by making township 'self-raised funds' — profits and fees from collective enterprises that could be at least half of local revenue in some places — public rather than discretionary local resources.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Quantifies how large the off-budget local economy was; each closure of an off-budget channel forced localities toward the next one, ultimately land sales and LGFVs.
insights.locator: The 1994 fiscal reform did not entirely end the local extrabudgetary revenue problem

insights.claim: The 1998 Big 4 reform ended local influence over centrally owned banks by transferring local Big 4 managers' personal dossiers from local party organization departments to the banks' headquarters, removing the local veto over their appointments.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Personnel control, not ownership, was the real lever over Chinese bank lending — the generalizable tell for who actually directs credit in any Chinese institution.
insights.locator: Another big blow to local finance was the 1998 reform

insights.claim: The Big 4 personnel reform worked: local branches cut loans to excess-capacity sectors when the Xi administration pushed to reduce that investment, forcing provincial leaders to travel to Beijing to lobby bank headquarters rather than simply order local branches to keep lending.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Evidence that central credit directives actually transmit through the Big 4 — supporting the case that Beijing can execute supply-side cuts when it chooses.
insights.locator: The Big 4 reform was a big success

insights.claim: Even during the 2008 RMB 4 trillion stimulus, some local Big 4 managers openly defied local governments and refused to lend to local projects they judged too risky.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Big 4 branch-level credit discipline predates Xi-era centralization, implying stimulus transmission through the big banks has always been partially filtered by risk judgment.
insights.locator: But even as early as 2008

insights.claim: Beijing telegraphed the Big 4 reform in advance with two credible signals: the 1995 Commercial Banking Law establishing that the Big 4 would act as genuine commercial institutions, and the 1994 creation of all three policy banks — China Development Bank, Agricultural Development Bank of China and Export-Import Bank of China — to take over policy lending.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Beijing signals major financial reforms years ahead through legal and institutional groundwork — track new institution creation as the leading indicator of the next reform.
insights.locator: The first signal was de jure

insights.claim: China's core development dilemma is that the center must maintain economic control and discipline while simultaneously sustaining local incentives and capacity for development, two objectives that are in clear tension.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The master framework for reading any Chinese policy cycle: every centralization must be paid for, and if the payment is absent, local growth effort collapses.
insights.quote: The center needs to maintain economic control and discipline but also simultaneously sustain local incentives and wherewithal for development. These two objectives are clearly in tension.
insights.locator: This contradiction is precisely China’s development dilemma

insights.claim: The Maoist period proves local incentives are decisive: the same Communist officials who drove local economic reform in the Deng era had failed to generate any comparable dynamism under a different incentive structure.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Personnel and institutions are constant; incentive design is the variable that determines Chinese growth — so watch cadre evaluation criteria, not GDP targets.
insights.locator: Those who doubt the importance of incentivizing local officials

insights.claim: Zhu Rongji should be recognized as the master architect of the 1990s reforms that catapulted China to the global center stage, and Deng Xiaoping's 1992 decision to bring him into the central leadership was prescient.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Historical benchmark for what a single technocrat with political cover can accomplish — the yardstick against which current Chinese economic leadership is measured.
insights.locator: Looking back at these reforms in the 1990s

insights.claim: Nostalgia for Zhu Rongji went viral on Chinese social media during Shanghai's draconian 2022 COVID lockdown, with articles recalling his effectiveness as Shanghai mayor in the late 1980s.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Public nostalgia for a competent technocrat is a soft but real signal of domestic dissatisfaction with current governance quality — relevant to China policy-risk sentiment.
